name: Chavismo
summary: Chavismo is the left-populist, Bolivarian movement built around Hugo Chávez and continued by Nicolás Maduro. It combines nationalism, Latin American integration and anti-imperialism with 'socialism of the 21st century': oil-funded social missions, nationalization, price controls and a communal state of participatory bodies, set against an 'oligarchy' and neoliberalism. It accepts private property alongside social property, and it is socially conservative on abortion and marriage.
scope: The mainstream Chavista project: Hugo Chavez's movement as the scholars Smilde and Azzellini define it ('left populist', 'Revolutionary Bolivarianism', socialism as its main symbolic discourse from 2005). Its own texts used are the 1999 Constitution, the Programa de la Patria (2013-2019), Chavez's 2012 Golpe de Timon and his UN speeches; the record is read through scholars such as Smilde and Wilpert. It excludes the pragmatic reprivatizing turn after Chavez, other Bolivarian-family movements and the wider pan-Latin socialism of the 21st century.

notes: Themes searched: economy and ownership, welfare and labour, property, democracy and participation, institutions, sovereignty and foreign policy, the UN, religion and family, race and indigenous peoples, environment, the armed forces and media. Almost every answer now rests on an article of the Constitution or on a scholar's account of the record; Wikipedia-based answers from the earlier pass were nulled where no primary or scholarly source states the position. Chavez's own texts (Programa de la Patria, Golpe de Timon, UN speeches) were read for economic and international themes; the scanned Programa extracts are garbled by columns, so answers on it are medium. Scholarly sources that were saved but yielded no direct statements (Tendencias, Polis, Green Left) are not cited. Positions are those of the Chavez-era mainstream; Madurismo is harder-line and Delcismo more pragmatic on markets.
